title: Amid fears of an AI bubble, cash may prove your only safe haven
full_text:
The most alarming feature of this year’s global sharemarket boom is not the obvious risk of an AI bubble but the lack of safe places for investors to put their money.
AI mania has infiltrated every corner of investment activity. Why did big super funds beat all rivals last year? Because they had the largest exposure to the artificial-intelligence boom.
Why did mining stocks save the ASX from going backwards? Because they rode the copper boom; copper being the metal crucial for AI data centres.
In short, traders are betting that AI will transform the world. But what if it fails to do so?
Or fails to do so in a reasonable timeframe?
Similar but different The last time investors faced a similar dilemma was during the final stages of the dotcom boom on Wall Street.
The dangers in 1999 were similar to today. A single narrative based on the possibilities of the internet had utterly overwhelmed the markets, leaving value investors on the sidelines.
The dotcom boom ended in 2000 with a mighty crash that sent global markets down by 50 per cent from peak to trough.
But back then Australian investors were more insulated from Wall Street. Most importantly, Wall Street mattered less. In 2000, US stocks represented about 49 per cent of the global market, whereas today it is close to 70 per cent.
What difference does that make? Well, flip that over, and we find that big super funds had about 20 per cent of their assets offshore at the time of the dotcom crash. Today, after years of chasing Wall Street returns, more than half of Australian super fund money is offshore.
And as always when markets are overheated, the value investors are sitting on the sidelines. Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway is waiting like a wolf with a record $US400bn ($570bn) to bargain hunt when the AI reversal inevitably hits.
Meanwhile, most professional investors sound increasingly frustrated. After taking a laudable swipe at “laughable IPO valuations”, Schroders head of Australian equities Martin Conlon put it like this during the week: “Certain ways to lose money longer-term are providing profit in the short term.” Conlon says he is “focused on business fundamentals and protecting capital rather than relying on cheap money propping up speculative excess”.
How can everyday investors similarly focus their investments? Certainly, most professional investors are showing no signs whatsoever of preparing for a downturn, which would typically be represented by building cash reserves to defend against a crash.
Morningstar associate director of manager research Steven Le says there has not been “any uplift in cash holding across fund managers at all”.
Bonds not the answer The biggest concern for the dutiful diversifier is that bonds – for so long the haven for conservative investors – are increasingly flawed as an alternative.
The corporate bond market is already becoming deeply skewed as the biggest raisings are linked with the AI-driven tech giants. For an investor who is primarily seeking a reliable return, this leaves only government bonds, which are safer but offer lower returns.
As well, the last time the sharemarket went backwards, in 2022, government bonds failed to offer the upside they were supposed to provide. The total return from the Australian government bond index that year was -11 per cent.
Since that time, bonds have been uninspiring – the five-year return of the Vanguard Australian Government Bond Index is close to zero.
Hamilton Wealth Partners founder Will Hamilton says “Australians never like bonds anyway”.
Gold loses its shine After bonds comes gold. But again, gold is not performing as a dependable safe haven of late.
Gold may ultimately play its part as a non-correlated asset, set to rise when markets drop, but the signs are mixed.
Even though we have seen six flat weeks on global sharemarkets, gold prices have been falling. Gold is down a whopping 25 per cent from its high point earlier in the year.
Some investors are trying to find diversification inside the sharemarket. A selection of A-REITs are selling at a discount to the wider market while, as the Australian research team at Canaccord Genuity points out: “Infrastructure continues to stand out for its defensive characteristics and reliable income.” But A-REITs such as Goodman have become proxy AI plays, while infrastructure spending in Australia will increasingly mean data centre construction. In fact, we are now seeing that AI data centre spending is competing with mining capital expenditure – this is a landmark for the wider economy, but no good for investors looking for diversification.
Cash is king In practice, it is very likely that most investors will depend on cash as the most reliable buffer for the day the bubble bursts.
If nothing else, cash returns are now beating inflation – cash rates are close to 5 per cent, and higher for term deposits, while inflation is closer to 4 per cent.
What’s more, your cash is government-guaranteed to the tune of $250,000 per person, per bank. As a side note, maybe it is time the government indexed that guarantee; it is nearly two decades since the global financial crisis.
Financial advisers are now increasingly concentrating on more sophisticated strategies for cash – not just having a useful amount on deposit but carefully doling out cash into longer-term deposits or, as a professional investor might say, “laddering the maturities”.
“You have six months locked in at 4.8 per cent and then 12 months at 5 per cent, and out from there perhaps five years at 5.34 per cent,” Sonas Group adviser Liam Shorte says.
“These are decent rates and they give people confidence.” A bit more confidence on how your portfolio would survive a major market reversal and a little less confidence in what Conlon calls “interplanetary revenues” might just be tonic for the year ahead.
